section.title: Joshua's Farewell
section.sectionRationale: Old and near death, Joshua gathers Israel's leaders for a farewell charge. He reminds them that the LORD fought for them and gave the land, and he presses one thing above all: hold fast to the LORD, love Him, obey His law, and do not turn to the gods of the nations. He warns that the same God who kept every good promise will bring disaster if they break the covenant. It is one movement, Joshua's farewell to the leaders, a solemn call to covenant faithfulness at the end of a faithful life.
section.thesis: Because the LORD faithfully fought for Israel and kept every promise, Joshua's dying charge is that they cling to Him alone in love and obedience, refusing the gods of the nations, for the God who blessed them will just as surely judge them if they forsake the covenant; His faithfulness cuts both ways.
section.frameNote: Three beats: the LORD has fought for you and will drive out the nations, verses 1 to 5; hold fast to the LORD and do not turn to other gods, verses 6 to 13; and God kept every promise, and will as surely judge covenant-breaking, verses 14 to 16.

units.label: The LORD has fought for you
units.note: it was the LORD your God who fought for you

verses.text: A long time after the LORD had given Israel rest from all the enemies around them, when Joshua was old and well along in years,
he summoned all Israel, including its elders, leaders, judges, and officers. “I am old and well along in years,” he said,
“and you have seen everything that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, because it was the LORD your God who fought for you.
See, I have allotted as an inheritance to your tribes these remaining nations, including all the nations I have already cut off, from the Jordan westward to the Great Sea.
The LORD your God will push them out of your way and drive them out before you, so that you can take possession of their land, as the LORD your God promised you.

units.label: Hold fast to the LORD and do not turn away
units.note: hold fast to the LORD your God; love Him

verses.text: Be very strong, then, so that you can keep and obey all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, not turning aside from it to the right or to the left.
So you are not to associate with these nations that remain among you. You must not call on the names of their gods or swear by them, and you must not serve them or bow down to them.
Instead, you shall {{davaq|hold fast}} to the LORD your God, as you have done to this day.
The LORD has driven out great and powerful nations before you, and to this day no one can stand against you.
One of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, just as He promised.
Therefore watch yourselves carefully, that you {{ahav|love}} the LORD your God.
For if you turn away and cling to the rest of these nations that remain among you, and if you intermarry and associate with them,

know for sure that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you. Instead, they will become for you a snare and a trap, a scourge in your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from this good land that the LORD your God has given you.

units.label: God kept every promise, and will as surely judge
units.note: not one promise has failed; likewise the calamity will come

verses.text: Now behold, today I am going the way of all the earth, and you know with all your heart and soul that not one of the good {{dabar|promises}} the LORD your God made to you has failed. Everything was fulfilled for you; not one promise has failed.

But just as every good thing the LORD your God promised you has come to pass, likewise the LORD will bring upon you the calamity He has threatened, until He has destroyed you from this good land He has given you.

If you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which He commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them, then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and you will quickly perish from this good land He has given you.”

davaq.gloss: To cling, hold fast, stick to, be joined to. The same word describes a man being joined to his wife, Genesis 2:24, and it is the heart of Joshua's charge: hold fast to the LORD your God. It calls for a clinging, covenant-loyal devotion to God alone, the opposite of clinging to the nations and their gods, verse 12, which uses the same verb.

ahav.gloss: To love. Joshua charges Israel to watch themselves carefully that they love the LORD their God. Covenant faithfulness is not cold rule-keeping but love; the same call stands at the heart of the law, love the LORD your God with all your heart, Deuteronomy 6:5, and Jesus names it the greatest commandment. Obedience flows from love for God.

dabar.gloss: A word, promise, matter. Joshua declares that not one good dabar of all the LORD promised has failed. The same reliability of God's word that made the good promises come true will make the threatened calamity come true if Israel breaks covenant; God's word is faithful in blessing and in warning alike, so it must be heeded.

basic.context: Years have passed since the conquest, and Joshua is now very old. Like Moses before him, he gathers Israel's leaders to give a farewell charge. His message is simple and urgent. First, remember: it was the LORD who fought for you and gave you this land; He will finish driving out the remaining nations. Second, therefore hold fast to the LORD, love Him, obey His law, and above all do not mix with the surrounding nations or worship their gods. Third, a sober warning: just as God kept every single good promise He made, so He will just as certainly bring the disaster He warned of if Israel breaks the covenant and turns to idols. Joshua stakes everything on God's faithfulness, which blesses the obedient and judges the unfaithful. The question underneath is: how do God's people stay faithful once the great victories are past and the pressure of comfort and compromise sets in?
basic.hermeneutics: This is historical narrative, a covenant farewell speech in the pattern of Deuteronomy. Its warnings about intermarriage and the nations are covenant-specific to Israel, aimed at guarding pure worship of the LORD, not a general rule about ethnicity; the danger was spiritual, being drawn into idolatry. The enduring lessons are the call to wholehearted love and loyalty to God, the danger of compromise with the surrounding culture's gods, and the truth that God's faithfulness cuts both ways, blessing and judgment.
basic.originalLanguages: Joshua's central charge is to davaq, to hold fast, to cling, to the LORD, and to ahav, to love, Him. And he grounds it in the reliability of God's dabar, His word: not one good promise failed, so the warned calamity will just as surely come if they break covenant.
basic.typology: Joshua's charge to hold fast and love the LORD points to the greater Joshua's summary of the law, to love God with all one's heart. And the warning that covenant-breaking brings judgment, later fulfilled in exile, points to the need for a Savior who keeps the covenant on His people's behalf and writes God's law on their hearts.
basic.christ: Joshua, near death, calls Israel to cling to the LORD, but Israel's later history shows they could not keep the covenant, and the threatened calamity of exile came. This drives us to Christ, who perfectly loved and obeyed the Father, kept the covenant for us, bore the curse of covenant-breaking, and gives His people a new heart to love and hold fast to God.
basic.god: God is the faithful warrior who fought for Israel and kept every promise. He is worthy of exclusive, loving devotion, jealous for His people's whole-hearted loyalty. And He is just: the same faithfulness that brought every blessing will bring judgment if His people forsake Him. His character is consistent in mercy and in justice.
basic.crossReferences: Deuteronomy 6 commands loving the LORD with all one's heart. Deuteronomy 28 lays out the blessings and curses of the covenant. Matthew 22 names love for God the greatest commandment. And Jeremiah 31 promises a new covenant with the law written on the heart.
basic.oneStory: At the end of his life, Joshua charges Israel to hold fast to the LORD and love Him, grounding the call in God's perfect faithfulness, which blesses the obedient and judges the unfaithful. The warning, later fulfilled in exile, points beyond itself to Christ, who keeps the covenant His people could not and writes God's law on their hearts so they can truly cling to Him.

context.literary:
Chapter 23 is built as a single, unbroken speech, unusual in a book otherwise dominated by battle reports and city lists, and its structure mirrors the covenant speeches of Deuteronomy that Joshua, as Moses' successor, is deliberately echoing. It moves through three movements that each open with a form of remembering, you have seen, verse 3, watch yourselves, verse 11, and you know, verse 14, so that memory, exhortation, and warning build on each other rather than standing as separate points. The refrain not one word has failed, verse 14, is a near verbatim recollection of 21:45, and its return here binds the whole second half of the book to its first half's great theological claim, so that this speech reads less like a new idea than like Joshua drawing out the full implications of something already proven true.

The chapter is also the first of two farewells, since chapter 24 will restage much of the same material before a larger gathering at Shechem; commentators have long debated whether 23 and 24 record two distinct occasions or two literary treatments of one, but either way the doubling itself is a literary choice, giving Joshua's last words the same kind of double emphasis Moses gives his own final instructions across Deuteronomy's long closing speeches and its closing Song.
context.historical:
Joshua speaks after what the text calls a long time of rest, verse 1, and near the very end of a life that will reach a hundred and ten years, 24:29, placing this speech within the same category as the great farewell addresses of Scripture, Jacob in Genesis 49, Moses in Deuteronomy, David in 1 Chronicles 28 to 29, all delivered by leaders who sense death approaching and use their last authority to bind a community to its founding commitments.

The nations Joshua still calls remaining, verse 4, were real political and religious entities whose continued presence created ongoing pressure toward intermarriage and religious compromise, exactly the danger that materializes within the period of the Judges within a generation of this speech, Judges 2:11 to 13 and 3:5 to 6. The vivid covenant curse imagery of verse 13, a snare, a trap, a scourge in the sides, thorns in the eyes, borrows the same structure common across ancient treaty documents, in which a suzerain's blessings and dangers to a vassal were spelled out in equally vivid, often bodily, terms, so that Israel's leaders would have recognized the form even before hearing the content.
context.canonical:
This speech stands squarely in the blessing and curse tradition of Deuteronomy 28 to 30, and its warning is not left to hang unresolved; Judges 2:11 to 15 records the very unfaithfulness Joshua warned against beginning almost immediately after his own generation dies, and by the fall of Samaria and Jerusalem the full calamity, exile from the good land, has overtaken both the northern and the southern kingdoms exactly as threatened here. Few chapters in the Old Testament have their warnings so precisely fulfilled by the Bible's own later history.

Yet the chapter's positive charge, hold fast and love the LORD, also becomes one thread the New Testament gathers up directly. Jesus is asked which is the greatest commandment and answers, unprompted, with the very words this speech assumes as foundational, to love the Lord your God with all your heart, Matthew 22:37 to 38, showing that Joshua's charge was never a peculiarly Israelite demand but the single center of the whole law. And where Joshua could only warn a people who would go on to fail, Jeremiah promises a coming day when God Himself will put His law within them and write it on their hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, and Ezekiel promises a new spirit that will move people to walk in God's statutes, Ezekiel 36:26 to 27, addressing exactly the gap this speech leaves open, a command Israel could hear but not, on its own, keep.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Joshua's own stated purpose is remembrance turned to resolve: he wants Israel's leaders to trace every victory back to its true cause, it was the LORD your God who fought for you, verse 3, so that gratitude rather than self-congratulation becomes the emotional foundation for what follows. Once that foundation is laid, his purpose shifts to summons: watch yourselves carefully, love the LORD, do not turn to the right or the left, language that assumes obedience is not automatic but requires ongoing, deliberate vigilance from leaders who will soon have no Joshua to hold them accountable.

His final and most severe purpose is to make the warning as serious as the promise had been comforting. By pairing the identical claim, not one word has failed, with the threat that the same God will just as certainly bring the calamity He has spoken of, Joshua intends to close off any reading of God's past faithfulness as a guarantee against future consequences. He wants the generation after the conquest, comfortable and secure for the first time in memory, to hear that comfort itself is often exactly when covenant loyalty quietly erodes, and to take his own approaching death as the reason to decide their loyalty now, while his own witness and warning are still fresh.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Joshua's specific instructions not to intermarry with the remaining nations address a concrete, historically bounded danger, spiritual compromise through household gods brought in by foreign wives, not a general principle about ethnicity; Rahab, a Canaanite by birth, is welcomed permanently into Israel a few chapters earlier precisely because she turned to the LORD, showing the line drawn here is theological rather than racial. Applying this text today as a rule about who believers may marry, without attention to the underlying concern for shared worship, misreads what the chapter is actually guarding.

What does transfer without qualification is the speech's theology of divine consistency: a God who keeps every blessing He has spoken will keep every warning too, so that presuming on grace while quietly tolerating compromise is treated here as a serious miscalculation about God's character, not a minor inconsistency, a principle any reader in any era stands under.

debates.question: Why does Joshua so strongly warn against associating and intermarrying with the nations?

views.label: The danger was spiritual, not ethnic
views.case: The concern throughout is that the nations and their gods would draw Israel into idolatry, verse 7; the prohibition on intermarriage is aimed at the worship of other gods that foreign alliances brought, exactly the ruin that later overtook Solomon, so the issue is guarding pure worship of the LORD, not racial purity, and outsiders who embraced the LORD, like Rahab, were welcomed.

views.label: A guard for covenant identity in a critical era
views.case: At the vulnerable moment of settlement, surrounded by the very peoples under judgment for their idolatry, Israel needed a clear boundary to preserve its distinct covenant loyalty; the strong warning fenced the young nation from absorbing the practices that would dissolve its devotion to the LORD, a boundary tied to that redemptive-historical moment.

debates.bearing: Both readings agree the aim was to keep Israel faithful to the LORD alone; the warning targets idolatry and spiritual compromise, and it calls God's people in every age to guard whole-hearted devotion against the pull of the surrounding culture's gods.

debates.question: Does Joshua's warning that God will bring upon you the calamity describe an automatic mechanism, or God's own free, personal response to covenant breaking?

views.label: A covenantal mechanism built into the relationship itself
views.case: The language of verse 15, just as every good thing has come to pass, likewise the LORD will bring, treats blessing and calamity as two sides of a single, symmetrical structure already fixed by the covenant's own terms in Deuteronomy 28, so that once the condition, forsaking the LORD, is met, the consequence follows almost automatically, the way a treaty's own penalty clause activates once its condition is triggered.

views.label: God's own personal and patient response, not an impersonal mechanism
views.case: Verse 16 grounds the calamity explicitly in divine anger, then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, personal language rather than mechanical language, and the actual history that follows in Judges and Kings shows repeated cycles of patience, discipline, and restoration rather than one automatic strike, suggesting the warning describes how a personal, relational God responds to persistent unfaithfulness over time, not a switch that flips the moment it is broken.

debates.bearing: The two are not finally opposed, since a God who has bound Himself by covenant can be both utterly reliable, so that the outcome is as certain as a mechanism, and utterly personal, so that anger, patience, and eventual judgment are all genuinely His own response rather than an impersonal force running on its own.

study.originalLanguages:
Three words already carry the lexicon, davaq, ahav, and dabar, and the speech adds at least three more constructions worth tracing.

Joshua opens his central charge with chazaq, be very strong, verse 6, the identical word and grammatical form the LORD used to charge Joshua himself at the very start of the book, be strong and very courageous, 1:7. The word choice is deliberate: the command that once launched Joshua's own leadership is now handed, almost unchanged, to the generation that must carry on without him, as if strength for obedience, not merely for battle, was always the deeper meaning of the original charge.

That same verse pairs chazaq with sur, turning aside, to the right or to the left, a set formula that runs throughout Deuteronomy for covenant loyalty, Deuteronomy 5:32, 17:11, 17:20, 28:14, each time picturing the law as a single narrow road from which a traveler could easily drift without ever consciously choosing to leave it. Joshua's warning assumes drift, not open rebellion, is the ordinary way faithfulness is lost.

Verse 14 uses a dignified idiom for approaching death, going the way of all the earth, the same phrase David will use for his own end, 1 Kings 2:2, a euphemism gentler than dying yet no less final, framing Joshua's entire speech as a testament spoken with full awareness of its own last-ness.

And running underneath the whole speech is the doubled use of dabar for both promise and threat, not one good dabar failed, verse 14, but the LORD will bring upon you the calamity, using a different noun, raah, evil or disaster, in verse 15, the very word that stands opposite tov, good, throughout the Hebrew Bible's most basic moral vocabulary, Genesis 2:9 and 2:17. The speech's entire argument rests on this pairing: the God whose tov, His good word, proved utterly reliable is the same God whose raah, His warned disaster, must be taken with the same seriousness, since one God stands behind both nouns.

Cling, love, be strong, do not turn aside, and reckon good and disaster with equal seriousness: Joshua's Hebrew vocabulary, more than any single doctrine stated outright, is what carries the covenant's full weight into this final address. No other chapter in the book leans this hard on so few, so carefully chosen roots.

typology.type: The call to hold fast to and love the LORD alone
typology.fulfillment: Jesus is asked, teacher, which is the greatest commandment in the law, and answers without hesitation, love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind, naming the very demand Joshua presses on Israel's leaders here, Matthew 22:36 to 38. The type escalates because Joshua could only command a love Israel's history shows it did not sustain, while John can say of believers, we love because He first loved us, 1 John 4:19, locating the origin of the love commanded in a prior love that actually creates it in the one commanded.

typology.type: The warning that covenant breaking brings judgment and exile
typology.fulfillment: Joshua's warning, if you transgress the covenant, the anger of the LORD will burn against you, verse 16, becomes Israel's own later history almost without alteration, culminating in exile from the very land this book records them entering. Paul declares that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, quoting Deuteronomy's own curse language. The type escalates because the calamity Joshua warned of fell, in history, on the guilty themselves, while the curse Christ bore fell on One who had broken no covenant at all, so that the warned disaster becomes, for those in Him, a disaster already exhausted.

typology.type: A covenant Israel could not keep
typology.fulfillment: The people who will hear this speech, and the generation after them, are precisely the people described in Judges as forsaking the LORD to serve the Baals within a single lifetime, Judges 2:11 to 13, proving that hearing the warning was never the same as heeding it. Jeremiah promises the remedy Joshua's speech could not supply, a new covenant, not like the one their fathers broke, in which God's law is put within them and written on their hearts, Jeremiah 31:31 to 33. The type escalates from a covenant that depended on human resolve holding fast, and did not hold, to a covenant secured entirely by God's own initiative, needing no human resolve to originate it, only to receive it.

typology.type: Joshua, dying, hands leadership to a covenant community without a mediator
typology.fulfillment: Joshua's death approaches with no successor named in this speech, only a summons to the leaders and elders themselves to hold the whole nation to its word, a genuinely fragile arrangement that Judges shows collapsing within a generation, everyone did what was right in his own eyes, Judges 21:25. Hebrews contrasts every mediator who must eventually die and hand off to someone else with Jesus, who continues forever and holds His priesthood permanently, because He always lives to make intercession, Hebrews 7:23 to 25. The type escalates from a leader whose departure genuinely endangers the covenant's future to a Mediator whose presence with His people never ends, so that the anxiety built into every farewell speech in Scripture finds its final answer in someone who never leaves.

study.christ:
Joshua's farewell is built to expose a gap that only Christ can close. He commands Israel's leaders to hold fast to the LORD and love Him with all their heart and soul, verses 8 and 11, and centuries later Jesus names loving God with all your heart, soul, and mind as the greatest commandment of all, Matthew 22:37 to 38, showing that Joshua was never asking for anything less, or other, than the very heart of the law itself. But Joshua can only command this love; he cannot create it. Israel's own history supplies the proof, within a single generation of leaders who had personally seen God's works, the next generation did not know the LORD or the work He had done for Israel, Judges 2:10, and the very unfaithfulness Joshua warned against in this chapter arrives almost immediately after his own death.

That gap between a real command and an unreal capacity to keep it drives the whole speech toward the gospel. Joshua's warning that covenant breaking brings the LORD's burning anger is fulfilled in Israel's exile, but it is answered, not merely fulfilled, at the cross, where Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, Galatians 3:13, taking upon Himself precisely the calamity Joshua warned this generation to fear. And where Joshua could only appeal to human resolve, watch yourselves carefully, God Himself promises through Jeremiah to supply what resolve alone could never sustain, I will put My law within them and write it on their hearts, Jeremiah 31:33, a new covenant in which obedience flows from a changed heart rather than a repeated warning.

Joshua also models Christ by contrast in his own person. He is a faithful mediator whose usefulness ends at death, so this speech is itself an admission that Israel's covenant now depends on leaders who will also, in time, fail and die. Hebrews draws the needed contrast, the former priests were prevented by death from continuing in office, but Jesus holds His priesthood permanently, because He continues forever, and He is always able to save those who draw near to God through Him, since He always lives to intercede for them, Hebrews 7:23 to 25. Joshua's farewell asks Israel to hold on without him after this day; Christ's own words to His disciples promise the opposite, and surely I am with you always, to the very end of the age, Matthew 28:20.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is first of all a warrior who fights and then withdraws to let His people rest, credited by Joshua for every victory in terms that leave no room for human boasting, it was the LORD your God who fought for you, verse 3, and one of you can put a thousand to flight, because the LORD your God fights for you, verse 10. Success this total, against nations this strong, is presented as proof of character rather than of Israel's own skill, a God whose power is real enough that its absence, if He ever withdrew it, would be immediately obvious.

He is also, in the same breath, a God who demands and deserves undivided love, not merely correct behavior; watch yourselves carefully, that you love the LORD your God, verse 11, treats affection, not only obedience, as the measure of faithfulness, and His jealousy over that love is not petty possessiveness but the appropriate response of a God who has, in fact, done everything for a people who did nothing to earn it.

He is unshakably consistent, and this consistency is the chapter's most sobering revelation. The same God who kept every good promise without exception will, Joshua insists, keep every warned disaster with the same exactness, so that His faithfulness is not selectively comforting; it applies with equal force to blessing and to judgment, and presuming that grace already given guarantees grace regardless of future unfaithfulness is exposed here as a serious misreading of who God actually is.

Finally, He is a God who works through means that can fail even while He Himself does not. Joshua's speech, urgent and personal as it is, cannot itself guarantee the outcome it demands, and Scripture is honest enough to record that outcome failing within a generation. The chapter therefore reveals a God whose own faithfulness is never in question even when the faithfulness of the human instruments meant to carry His warnings forward plainly is, a tension the rest of Scripture resolves only by God taking up, in Christ, the very obedience His people could not sustain on their own.

crossReferences.note: Israel's daily confession, hear, O Israel, the LORD is our God, the LORD is one, and you shall love the LORD your God with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your strength, is the command Joshua's whole charge assumes as already known; he is not introducing a new demand but insisting an old, central one still be kept now that the conquest is finished.

Chapter 21 already declared that not one of all the LORD's good promises to the house of Israel had failed. Joshua repeats the identical claim here almost word for word, showing that his warning about coming judgment is built on the very same foundation as his earlier confidence about God's blessing, not on a different or lesser view of God.

Within a single generation after Joshua's own death, a generation arose who did not know the LORD or what He had done for Israel, and they served the Baals, forsaking the God of their fathers. This is the precise unfaithfulness Joshua warns against in this chapter, arriving with almost no delay at all.

Moses had already spelled out, at length, the disasters that would follow covenant breaking, beginning with the same word Joshua uses here, calamity or curse, coming upon a disobedient nation. Joshua's brief warning in a few verses assumes his listeners already know the fuller, harsher list Moses gave a generation earlier.

Paul declares that Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, quoting Deuteronomy's own curse language. The calamity Joshua warns Israel to fear here is, in the end, the very curse Christ absorbs on behalf of everyone who trusts Him.

God promises a coming covenant unlike the one Israel broke, in which He will put His law within His people and write it on their hearts, so that all will know Him. This is the remedy for the exact gap Joshua's farewell leaves open, a command Israel could hear plainly but could not, in the end, keep on its own strength.

God promises to remove the heart of stone from His people and give a new spirit that moves them to walk in His statutes. Where Joshua could only say watch yourselves carefully, Ezekiel foresees a work of God that actually enables the careful watching Joshua could only demand.

Asked to name the greatest commandment, Jesus answers with the very demand Joshua issues here, to love the Lord your God with all your heart, all your soul, and all your mind, confirming that Joshua's farewell was never a lesser, merely national requirement but a statement of the law's true center.

As David's own death approaches, he tells Solomon, I am about to go the way of all the earth, be strong and act like a man, echoing both Joshua's idiom for death and his charge to be strong, so that Israel's history keeps repeating this same scene, a dying leader summoning the next generation to faithfulness he can no longer enforce.

study.oneStory:
This speech sits at a genuine hinge in the story. Behind it lies a completed, God-given conquest, the fulfillment of promises stretching back to Abraham; ahead of it lies the period of the Judges, in which nearly everything Joshua warns against here comes true within a single generation. The chapter's placement is not incidental: it is the Bible's own way of marking that grace received does not, by itself, guarantee grace sustained, a truth the whole Old Testament will go on demonstrating through cycle after cycle of blessing, drift, judgment, and rescue.

Joshua's charge to hold fast and love the LORD is, in miniature, the whole law compressed into a farewell, and its failure to hold, documented so quickly in Judges, is exactly why the Old Testament keeps building toward something more than another Joshua. Every subsequent leader who hands off power, Samuel, David, Solomon, faces the identical question this chapter raises, what happens when the one holding the people together is no longer there, and every answer within the Old Testament proves temporary, since every leader eventually dies exactly as Joshua does two verses after this speech ends, 24:29.

The New Testament announces the permanent answer. Where covenant loyalty in Joshua's day depended on a nation's own resolve to watch themselves carefully, the new covenant depends on God's own resolve to change the heart that resolves, Jeremiah 31:33 and Ezekiel 36:26 to 27. Where Joshua's departure left Israel dependent on elders who would also die, Christ's own departure comes with a promise no farewell speech in the Old Testament could make, I am with you always, to the very end of the age, Matthew 28:20. And where the calamity Joshua warned of finally fell on a rebellious nation carried into exile, the greater calamity of the broken covenant falls, at the cross, on the only Man who never once turned aside to the right or to the left, so that everyone who holds fast to Him is held, finally, by someone who cannot die and leave them again.

quiz.q: What did Joshua remind Israel was the reason for their victories?

options.text: That it was the LORD their God who fought for them.
options.note: Verses 3 and 10 credit all the victories to the LORD fighting for Israel.

options.text: That their army was superior to the nations.
options.note: Joshua credits the LORD, not Israel's military strength, for the victories.

options.text: That the nations were weak and disorganized.
options.note: The nations were great and powerful; the victory came because the LORD fought for Israel.

options.text: That Joshua's own leadership won the wars.
options.note: Joshua points to the LORD, not himself, as the one who fought for them.

quiz.q: What was the heart of Joshua's charge to Israel?

options.text: To hold fast to the LORD and love Him, refusing the gods of the nations.
options.note: Verses 6 to 11 call Israel to cling to and love God alone.

options.text: To expand their territory by any means necessary.
options.note: God would drive out the nations, but the charge was loyal love to God, not territorial ambition.

options.text: To build a grand temple immediately.
options.note: The charge was covenant faithfulness, not temple-building, which came generations later.

options.text: To make alliances with the surrounding nations.
options.note: The opposite: he warned them not to associate with the nations or their gods.

quiz.q: How does Joshua use God's faithfulness in his warning?

options.text: As God kept every good promise, so He will surely bring the threatened calamity if they break the covenant.
options.note: Verses 14 to 16 show God's faithfulness cuts both ways, in blessing and in judgment.

options.text: He argues that God's faithfulness means they can never face judgment.
options.note: The opposite: the same faithfulness that blessed will also judge covenant-breaking.

options.text: He says God's promises might or might not come true.
options.note: Joshua stresses not one promise failed; God's word is certain, in blessing and warning alike.

options.text: He claims God's warnings are only empty threats.
options.note: Joshua treats the warnings as certain to be fulfilled, just as the promises were.

quiz.q: How does Joshua's charge point beyond itself to Christ?

options.text: Israel could not keep the covenant, so it points to Christ, who kept it for us, bore its curse, and writes God's law on our hearts.
options.note: The unkept covenant drives us to Christ and the new covenant, Galatians 3:13 and Jeremiah 31:33.

options.text: It proves people can keep God's covenant perfectly by trying harder.
options.note: Israel's later failure shows they could not; the answer is Christ, not mere effort.

options.text: It shows God's law does not really matter.
options.note: God's law matters deeply; the point is that Christ fulfills it and enables obedience.

options.text: It has no connection to Christ.
options.note: The unkept covenant and the promised calamity point clearly to Christ, who keeps the covenant and bears its curse.

questions: Joshua urged Israel to hold fast to the LORD once the great victories were behind them. Where are you most tempted to drift from God in seasons of comfort and ease?
The charge was to love God, not merely to obey rules. Would you describe your walk with God more as loving devotion or as cold duty, and what would deepen your love for Him?
Joshua warned against being drawn into the worship and ways of the surrounding culture. Which of the culture's gods, success, comfort, approval, most tempts your loyalty away from God?
God's faithfulness means both His promises and His warnings come true. How does taking God's warnings as seriously as His promises change the way you live?

Joshua could command love and loyalty, but only Christ can create them by writing God's law on the heart. How does resting in Christ, who kept the covenant for you, free and fuel your own faithfulness?

translationNotes.note: Hold fast renders davaq, to cling or be joined; the same verb appears in verse 12 for clinging to the nations, sharpening the contrast between loyalty to God and to idols.
A snare, a scourge in your sides, and thorns in your eyes is vivid covenant-curse imagery for the trouble the un-driven-out nations would bring, fulfilled in Judges.
Going the way of all the earth is a dignified way of speaking of approaching death; the phrase frames Joshua's words as a farewell testament, like Moses' in Deuteronomy.
